parole.significato: stable, stall (building where horses or the like are kept)
parole.testo: From Byzantine Greek στάβλος (stáblos), στάβλον (stáblon), from Latin stabulum.
Borrowed from Byzantine Greek σπόρτυλον (spórtulon), borrowed from Latin sportula.

parole.significato: a kind of wide storage pot of glass or clay
parole.testo: From the toponym بَرْنِيق (barnīq, “Benghazi”) due to some source materials having been produced there, cognate to French vernis, English varnish, and particularly to certain southern Middle French names for a vase or platter breingal, beringuier, bernigant, bernigal, barnigal, vernigal, in obsolete

parole.significato: post, mail, an institution to send messages, intelligence
parole.testo: Borrowed from Byzantine Greek βέρηδος (bérēdos), from Ancient Greek βέρεδος (béredos), borrowed from Latin verēdus, borrowed from Gaulish *werēdos, from Proto-Celtic *uɸoreidos, from *uɸo- + *reidos. First attested in the 6th century.

parole.significato: a kind of piece of fine silk for clothing
parole.testo: From Byzantine Greek βυσσίνη (bussínē) from βύσσος (bússos). See also بَزّ (bazz) and بِزَّة (bizza).
A more popular variant of the original مَقْدُونِس (maqdūnis, “parsley; Macedonian coriander”), ultimately from Byzantine Greek μακεδονήσιον (makedonḗsion, “Macedonian (herb)”).

parole.significato: tassel, puff, a cord or belt garnished with beads and other jewellery, or other cable
parole.testo: From Byzantine Greek ἡγουμένη (hēgouménē), at first passed as جُمِّنِيَا (jumminiyā), جُمَّلِيّة (jummaliyya), a name applied to leading ropes; though also connected to Persian کمان (kamân, “anything bent”).

parole.significato: to register, enter, make an entry
parole.testo: The noun is from Byzantine Greek σιγίλλιον, σιγίλλον (sigíllion, sigíllon), from Latin sigillum (“seal; sealed document”); attested also as Classical Syriac ܣܝܓܝܠܝܘܢ , ܣܓܠܐ (sagīlā, sīgīlīōn). The verb is denominal. or MPers. sang-gil.

Borrowed from Byzantine Greek σίτλα (sítla).

From Byzantine Greek σιγιλλᾶτος (sigillâtos), σιγιλλᾶτον (sigillâton), from Latin sigillātus (literally “sealed”), the epithet of some kind of fabric, since sealings are most iconically of red colour.

parole.significato: a lower-tier provincial official assisting in tax-gathering
parole.testo: Borrowed from Byzantine Greek σύμμαχος (súmmakhos).
From Byzantine Greek ἀρχιδιάκονος (arkhidiákonos), ἀρχιδιάκων (arkhidiákōn, “archdeacon”), or a more corrupt colloquial form, compare شُرْطَة (šurṭa) for χ (kh) → ش (š).

parole.significato: vanguard, choice men of the army
parole.testo: From regional Byzantine Greek χόρτη (khórtē), χώρτη (khṓrtē), elsewhere also κόρτη (kórtē), κόρτης (kórtēs), κώρτη (kṓrtē), κώρτης (kṓrtēs), κοόρτη (koórtē), κοόρτης (koórtēs), from Latin cohors.
A vessel already known to the Ṭūlūnids from Byzantine Greek σανδάλιον (sandálion) having both the ship and the shoe sense, diminutive of σάνδαλον (sándalon).

parole.significato: territorial tax, property tax, known in (historical) al-Andalus and Egypt, taking the place of the original kharaj poll…
parole.testo: Occurring from the mid-8th century onwards, from Byzantine Greek τάβλα (tábla), τάβλη (táblē), τάβλον (táblon), from Latin tābula. Doublet of طَاوُلَة (ṭāwula).

parole.significato: a piece of paper or skin on which something is written, roll of papyrus, scroll
parole.testo: Borrowed from Byzantine Greek τομάριον (tomárion).
Borrowed from Byzantine Greek φοσσᾶτον (phossâton), borrowed from Latin fossātum.
From the plural of Byzantine Greek φλασκίον (phlaskíon), from Latin flascō, from Proto-Germanic *flaskǭ. Later perhaps reborrowed in the Alexandrine port from Italian fiaschetta.
Borrowed from Byzantine Greek φανάριον (phanárion).
From Byzantine Greek κάμπανος (kámpanos), γάμπανος (gámpanos), from Latin campāna.
Borrowed from Byzantine Greek κοντάκιον (kontákion), diminutive of Byzantine Greek κόνταξ (kóntax, “pole”), diminutive of κοντός (kontós, “pole”).

parole.significato: a unit of capacity unclear in extent
parole.testo: Borrowed from Byzantine Greek κάγκελλον (kánkellon), itself from Old Persian.

From Byzantine Greek κονδοῦρα (kondoûra, “cutter”), originally referring to a kind of post-horse. For the word for “shoe” widespread in the dialects, it is supposedly only from Ottoman Turkish قوندورا (kundura) that it was acquired.
Borrowed from Byzantine Greek μειζότερος (meizóteros).

parole.significato: must, fermentation grapes, or recently-made wine
parole.testo: Borrowed from Byzantine Greek μουστάριον (moustárion, “a measure of must”), from Latin mustārium (“a measure of must”), from Latin mustum (“must”).
Possibly borrowed from Byzantine Greek ἀλμενιχιακά (almenikhiaká, “astronomical indexes”), possibly from Coptic.

parole.significato: various kinds of cloth, textile covering
parole.testo: Borrowed from Byzantine Greek μανδίλιον (mandílion), μαντίλιον (mantílion), or μανδήλη (mandḗlē, “cloth, hand towel, handkerchief, tablecloth”), from Latin mantēlium, mantēle (“cloth, hand towel, handkerchief, tablecloth”). Also vocalized hyper-classically مِنْدِيل (mindīl) at odds with standard usa

From Byzantine Greek μεταφυσική (metaphusikḗ), from the title of the collection by Aristotle μετὰ τὰ φυσικά (metà tà phusiká), a collection that comes after (μετά (metá)) Aristotle's collection entitled τὰ φυσικά (tà phusiká), from φυσικός (phusikós, “natural”).
